title: Pray differently
hookLine: pray not "let me get this" but "let me not crave it," not "let me be rid of it" but "let me not fear" (Meditations 9.40)

cards: Late at night, the asking comes. Let the test come back clear. Let me get the job.
Let this pain go away. Let my kid be okay. People of every faith, and people of none, find themselves sending wishes like these out into the dark.
Marcus did too. Near the end of book nine he wrote a short reflection on his own prayers, and it turns the asking around.

teach.h: EITHER THE GODS CAN, OR THEY CAN'T.
teach.b: Either the gods have power or they don't, Marcus writes. If they don't, why pray at all?

If they do, why not pray for the power not to fear these things, not to crave them, not to grieve over them, rather than praying only that they come or don't come? Someone might say: the gods put that in my own power.

teach.h: USE WHAT'S IN YOUR POWER, FREELY.
teach.b: Then, Marcus answers, isn't it better to use what's in your power with freedom than to strain like a slave after what isn't? And who told you the gods don't help us even with what's in our power? Then his examples.
One person prays: how can I win that woman? You: how can I stop wanting to? Another: how can I be rid of this?
You: how can I stop needing to be rid of it?

teach.h: NOT LOSE HIM, OR NOT FEAR LOSING HIM.
teach.b: Another: how can I not lose my little son? You: how can I not be afraid to lose him? Turn your prayers this way, he says, and see what comes.

teach.h: HIS OWN PRAYERS, NO ONE ELSE'S.
teach.b: Marcus is writing to himself, a Stoic, about his own prayers, not anyone else's.
People in many traditions pray for healing and for their children, and many also pray for courage and peace in the same breath. And the little son is not abstract.
Marcus and his wife Faustina lost a number of their children young.

how: Readers who take up this entry often notice the fear or craving beneath a hope, and those who pray sometimes ask for steadiness alongside the outcome they want, in the words of their own tradition.

o: give up prayer and rely on yourself alone
pray in a new language or a new place each day
ask not only for the outcome, but freedom from fear

p: pray not to fear, crave, or grieve
not lose him, or not fear losing him

s: Marcus tells everyone to stop praying for outcomes
he's writing to himself about his own prayers, and speaks for no one else's.
in his third example, one person prays not to lose a son, and Marcus prays not to fear losing him
that's the last of his three examples.

games.q: you're Marcus. your little son is sick. how does his notebook say to turn the prayer?
o: how can I not lose him?
how can I not be afraid to lose him?
games.why: he contrasts asking not to lose his little son with asking not to be afraid of losing him. Marcus and Faustina lost a number of their children young.

practice: Name one wish you've been carrying, and hold it honestly; you don't have to give it up. Underneath it, notice the fear or the craving that comes with it.
If you pray, you might bring both, the wish and the calm, in whatever words your own tradition gives you; if you don't, simply hold the turn: less fear of this.

wordCard.voice: Pray differently. Marcus's turn: not only let me get this, but let me not crave it; not only save me from this, but let me not fear it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I pray, I ask, I wish. Marcus's turn changes what the asking is for.

carryVoice: Your line: let me not fear. The wish can stay; the fear can loosen. Until tomorrow.
